chapter_theme: Poems 101-120 move from Avvai's praise of Athiyaman and his son, the bard's trust in a patron and the warning not to slight a young king, to Kapilar on Pari: his giving, the siege of Parambu by the three crowned kings, and the laments of Pari's daughters and his poet after his death.

101.reading: Avvai tells her own heart that Athiyaman greets a bard on the hundredth visit, even with a crowd, as eagerly as on the first, so whether the gift comes late or soon it is as sure as the food-ball an elephant holds between its tusks, and the heart need not fret.
101.nuance: The colophon files it as a demand for the gift (பரிசில் கடா நிலை), but the poem turns the demand inward: the one being urged to wait is the poet's own hungry heart. The food-ball is in the elephant's own keeping and already between its tusks, so the image says the gift is decided and only the moment is open. Line 9 (அருந்தே மாந்த) can be divided more than one way; the sense of a heart greedy for its meal is the likeliest.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is a bard reassuring herself about a patron's gift

comparisons.tenor: the gift the patron has already resolved to give

102.reading: The prince is compared to the spare axle that salt-carters tie under a heavily loaded cart drawn by young, unbroken bulls, for the climbs and drops of the road, and to the full moon, so that no darkness can come to those who live in his shade.
102.nuance: The first image is of a prince who is not yet needed: a spare axle does nothing until the young bulls stumble and the main axle breaks, so the praise is that of a son held in reserve during his father's reign. The poem names no one; the patron, Athiyaman's son Pokuttezhini, comes from the colophon.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the prince as the people's reliable reserve

comparisons.tenor: the prince on whom his people fall back
the prince, who drives off darkness for his dependants

103.reading: Avvai tells a viraliyar sitting at the start of the wasteland road, with a one-headed drum at one end of her pole and a small hollow drum at the other, asking who will turn up her upturned bowl, that Anji is not far: he is in enemy country among his young elephants and the smoke of burning villages, and even in a dry season he can keep her bowl full of soft fat-rich food.
103.nuance: The patron is found not at home but at the front, so the bard is sent toward war smoke; the poem makes his generosity and his raids one fact, since the fat that fills her bowl comes from the enemy's land.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer is directed to a patron, the guide-poem situation

comparisons.tenor: the dark smoke of the burning war-front around his elephants

104.reading: Avvai warns the enemy warriors: if you look down on my lord as a youth, not weighing his many subtle deeds, you will not win, for he is like the crocodile that drags down and kills an elephant in a foot-deep pool where village boys play.
104.nuance: The water is made as small as possible (foot-deep, a children's pool), so the crocodile's strength owes nothing to its ground: the image answers both the scorn of youth and the scorn of a small domain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem asserts the king's martial worth against those who would scorn it

105.reading: Kapilar tells a bright-browed viraliyar that she will win fine jewels if she goes singing to Pari, whose gentleness is sweeter than the water that, rain or no rain, comes down every peak of his ladder-hung hill, carrying the cool petals of bee-haunted lilies over the wide horse-gram fields.
105.nuance: The water flows whether it rains or not, which already says what the poem will say of the giver; the comparison is of degree (sweeter than), so Pari's manner outdoes the one thing in his land that never fails. Line 5 (உழைகால் ஆட) is hard to construe; the run of the water over the fields is the likely sense.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer is sent to the patron

106.reading: As the gods do not refuse even the erukkam, with its clustered blossoms and poor leaves, neither good nor bad, when people offer it, so Pari's open hand holds itself bound to give even when the foolish and the weak come to him.
106.nuance: The comparison reverses the usual direction: the giver is set in the place of the god who receives offerings, and the asker in the place of the poor flower, so to be given to by Pari is to be accepted by him. கடவன் makes the gift a debt he owes, not a favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names the patron's giving as his defining nature

comparisons.tenor: the unworthy askers whom Pari still receives

107.reading: The fine-tongued poets praise one man, calling out 'Pari, Pari'; but Pari is not the only one: there is also the rain, which sustains this world.
107.nuance: It looks like a rebuke of the poets for flattering one man, and the rebuke is the praise: the only rival that can be found for him is the rain. The 'one' (ஒருவர், ஒருவனும்) is repeated so that the denial of uniqueness ends by granting it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron in the form of mock blame

comparisons.tenor: Pari, whose giving keeps the world as rain does

108.reading: Such is the Parambu the poets sing of: the dry-end firebrand a hill woman set burning is sandalwood, so its fragrant smoke drifts across to the flowering branches of the vengai on the slope; and Pari, having taken up virtue, would not say 'I will not come' if suppliants asked for him, but would be theirs.
108.nuance: In this land sandalwood is common firewood and its scent goes to the neighbouring tree unasked; the poem sets that scene beside the giver without saying they are alike, and leaves the reader to make the match. The last line goes past giving goods: asked for himself, he would go.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's readiness to give even himself

109.reading: Kapilar tells the three crowned kings besieging Parambu that it is to be pitied: drums and all, they cannot starve it, for it has four yields no ploughman sows (bamboo rice, jackfruit, valli tubers and honey), its hill is like the sky and its springs like the stars; tie elephants to every tree, spread chariots over every field, they will not take it by effort and he will not yield it to the sword; but if they tune small lutes and come singing and dancing with their viralis, he will give land and hill together.
109.nuance: The poem ends a siege argument with a guide-poem: the one road into the fort is the bard's road, so the kings are mocked by being offered the only means they cannot use without ceasing to be kings. The colophon's thurai speaks of refusing a daughter, which the poem itself never mentions.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is spoken from the besieged hill-fort against its besiegers

comparisons.tenor: the hill of Parambu, too vast to compass

110.reading: Even if you three kings join your conquering armies in anger, Parambu is hard to take; its cool good country has three hundred villages and the suppliants have already received all three hundred; there remain only Pari and I, and the hill: come singing and they are yours.
110.nuance: The arithmetic is the point: nothing is left to conquer because everything has already been given, so the kings are told they arrive after the bards. Kapilar counts himself with Pari among what remains (யாமும் பாரியும்).

thinai_evidence.note: the besieged side answers the besiegers

111.reading: The great dark hill is to be pitied: to win it with the spear is hard even for kings, but it is easy for a kinai-drummer's daughter whose kohl-lined eyes are like a pair of blue lilies, if she comes singing.
111.nuance: அளிதோ (pitiable) is said of the hill, which can be had so cheaply by the humblest singer and is so costly to kings; the pity and the boast are the same word.

thinai_evidence.note: the defended hill set against the besiegers' spears

112.reading: Pari's daughters say: that month, in that white moonlight, we had our father and no one had taken our hill; this month, in this white moonlight, kings with victorious drums have taken our hill, and we have no father.
112.nuance: The two halves use the same words in the same order, so the only change is the loss itself; திங்கள் is both the month and the moon, and the unchanging moonlight measures what has changed. The father is named first in the first half and last in the second.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead father and a lost home

113.reading: Kapilar says to Parambu: once you were our friend, opening toddy jars, felling dark rams and giving rice with rich meat relish as much as anyone wished; now Pari is dead, and bewildered and helpless, with streaming eyes, we worship and praise you and go, seeking husbands for the girls with small bangles and fragrant dark hair.
113.nuance: The hill, not the dead man, is addressed and called a friend (நட்டனை), so the farewell is to the place that fed the bards; the last two lines give the reason for leaving, the duty to the daughters.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament at leaving the dead patron's hill

114.reading: It can be seen from here and from the small hill beyond, surely: the hill of the tall one, where the courtyard runs wet with the dregs of pressed toddy, strewn like the food-balls an elephant chews and drops, and where chariots were given away from where he sat.
114.nuance: The hill is still visible from near and far, and that is the grief: the place stands while the giving is over. Only the colophon makes this a lament; the lines themselves are a picture of a feasting court.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament that looks back at the dead patron's hill

comparisons.tenor: the strewn dregs of pressed toddy

115.reading: On one side the waterfall roared, and on the other the clear honey-toddy, poured to fill the bards' bowls and spilled, ran washing over the stones: so it was once on the hill of the gentle one who was harsh to kings with many spears and great elephants.
115.nuance: மன்னே marks the whole scene as past; the toddy for bards is set as a second waterfall. The closing phrase, harsh to kings and sweet (இன்னான் ஆகிய இனியோன்), joins the two faces Pari showed to two kinds of visitor.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for what the hill was

comparisons.tenor: the toddy poured for bards running over the stones

116.reading: Kapilar grieves that the girls with lily garlands and rain-dark eyes now climb a heap of eecham leaves by a little hut with a thorn fence to count the salt-carters' carts, when once, from the high hill of their father Pari of strong toddy and sharp spear, a hill of unfailing plenty where peacocks danced, stags leapt and trees bore fruit out of season, they counted the golden-saddled horses of kings who came to war not knowing his strength.
116.nuance: The poem is built on one act, counting, done in two places: then the girls counted enemy horses from a fort that could not be taken, now they count passing salt carts from a hut. Line 14 (வியன்மலை அற்றே) may be 'like the broad hill' or 'the broad hill is gone'; our text also lacks a line the other edition has after line 9, so the middle of the poem is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over the dead patron's daughters

117.reading: Even when Saturn smokes, comets appear and Venus runs to the south, the land of the father of the girls with fine bangles was a dry upland where rain never failed: fields filled, bush flowers bloomed, wild cows that had calved by the houses grazed in long herds on good grass, the worthy multiplied under a straight sceptre, and mullai budded like a kitten-civet's sharp teeth.
117.nuance: The three opening signs are omens of drought, and the poem says they had no power over this land because of its ruler's justice, so a lord of a hill is given the crowned king's rain-making sceptre. The lament is only in the past tense and in the phrase 'the father of the girls'.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament that praises the dead patron's land

comparisons.tenor: the pointed buds of the mullai

118.reading: The land of cool Parambu, of Pari who gave chariots and whose strong shoulders wielded sharp spears, is now seeing its little clear-water tank, with a curved bank like the eighth-day moon and a head where rocks and ridges meet, breaking.
118.nuance: With no one to keep it, the tank, the land's store of water, gives way; the poem lets the breach of one small tank stand for the end of the whole country. கீள்வது (is breaking, is splitting) is the one word that carries the lament, and its exact sense is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over the ruin of the dead patron's land

comparisons.tenor: the curved bank of the tank

119.reading: In the pleasant season after the rains, when therul blossoms open like the spots on an elephant's face and the red anthill holes turn sour with winged termites, the land rich in soft millet: will it last? It is the land of the generous one who, like a lone tree on a long shadeless road, gave to suppliants beyond what drum-rich kings would give.
119.nuance: நந்துங் கொல்லோ can be heard as 'will it still flourish?' or 'will it perish?', and the doubt is the lament. The lone tree is valued because nothing else on the road gives shade, so the simile measures Pari against the kings as the tree against the bare road.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament asking whether the dead giver's land can endure

comparisons.tenor: the giver, the only shelter suppliants had

120.reading: On the red upland where the vengai grew, after the rains men ploughed again and again, sowed, harrowed and weeded until the millet rose tall like a peahen fresh from laying and bore grain top to bottom; then came the harvest of new varagu and millet, the bean pods ripe, buried toddy offered at every grass hut, and rice cooked with ghee and gram: will this effortless plenty last, the land of the father of the long-haired maidens, the war-hot lord of the high bamboo peaks whose quality poets never tire of singing?
120.nuance: The long account of farm labour ends in the word வருந்தா (without toil), so the plenty is called effortless just after the poem has shown the work; the lament turns on whether the work will still bear fruit without the lord. Several farm words (பல்லி, கவ்வை, பெருந் தோள் தாலம்) are rare and their sense is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament asking whether the dead patron's land can endure

links.note: Both Avvai on Athiyaman (101) and Kapilar on Pari (114) use the elephant's food-ball (கவளம்) as their simile: held safe between the tusks in 101, chewed and dropped in 114.
links.teaches: The same image of a patron's court serves praise and lament: in the living patron's poem the food-ball is the gift kept safe for the bard, and in the dead patron's poem it is the dropped leavings that mark where feasts used to be.

links.note: 101 argues at length that Athiyaman's gift never fails however long it is delayed; the akam poem 162 calls Athikan, of the same house, one who never let a suppliant's hope fail (நசைபிழைப்பு அறியா).
links.teaches: What 101 has to argue as a bard's private reassurance had become, in an akam poet's line, a fixed epithet of the Athiyaman house, so the praise poem shows the experience behind the epithet.

links.note: 102 likens the prince to the spare axle salt-carters (உமணர்) tie under a loaded cart; in 116 Pari's orphaned daughters climb a heap of leaves to count the salt-carters' carts going by.
links.teaches: The salt caravan stands for dependence on a protector in praise and for the loss of one in lament: in 102 the patron is the carters' reserve, in 116 his daughters have nothing to do but watch the carts that no longer concern them.

links.note: 103 is Avvai's guide poem sending a viraliyar to Anji; Akananuru 352 cites a bard's song that set down Anji's good fame (அஞ்சி நல்லிசை நிறுத்த) as a model of fine craft.
links.teaches: Read together they show the life of a praise song: Avvai directs performers to Anji, and a later akam poet can take a bard's song of Anji's fame as the standard of a well-made song, so the guide poems made the fame the akam poets borrowed.

links.note: Kural 495 says the crocodile wins in deep water and is killed by anything once out of it; 104 makes the young king a crocodile that kills an elephant in a foot-deep children's pool.
links.teaches: The Kural uses the crocodile to teach that strength belongs to the ground, while Avvai uses it to claim a strength that needs almost no ground, so a court poet's praise could deny the very limit the ethics book counsels kings to respect.

links.note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to slight him as young (இளையர்); 104 warns the enemy's warriors not to slight Avvai's lord as young (இளையன்).
links.teaches: The warning against scorning a young king is a rule of court conduct in the Kural and a battlefield threat in Avvai, which shows the same caution was voiced to subjects as duty and to enemies as danger.

links.note: Kural 221 calls giving only what goes to those who have nothing, all else being a measured exchange; 106 says Pari holds himself bound to give even to the foolish and the weak, as the gods accept even the erukkam flower.
links.teaches: The Kural defines true giving by the asker having nothing to return, and Kapilar supplies the image for it, the god who accepts a worthless flower, so the giver's duty is modelled on a god's acceptance rather than on a bargain.

links.note: Kural 211 says obligation seeks no return, for the world gives nothing back to the rain; 107 says Pari is not the only one, for the rain too sustains the world.
links.teaches: Kapilar's mock rebuke works only because the comparison of the giver with the rain was already accepted, as the Kural makes it a principle, so the joke assumes the doctrine and the doctrine has here a named man as its model.

links.note: Naladiyar 97 sets the rain and the world's doing what it should side by side as the two things the world survives by; 107 sets Pari and the rain side by side as sustainers of the world.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's pairing of rain with human giving is the background against which 107's line reads as praise, and 107 shows that pairing applied to one patron centuries before it was stated as a general rule.

links.note: Kural 223 praises giving without uttering the misery of 'I have nothing'; 108 says Pari would not say 'I will not come' even if suppliants asked for him.
links.teaches: The Kural forbids the giver one refusal, the plea of having nothing; 108 imagines the case past it, where nothing is left and the giver offers himself, so the poem tests the maxim at its limit.

links.note: 105 sends a viraliyar to Pari with the promise of jewels; 109 tells the besieging kings that the only way to take Parambu is to come as bards with their viralis behind them.
links.teaches: Kapilar turns his own guide-poem formula into siege terms: the road that brings a performer gifts is the only road into the fort, which shows the guide poem's convention used as a political weapon.

links.note: 109 says Parambu needs no ploughing because its hill yields four foods by itself; Akananuru 303 describes flocks of sparrows of Pari's Parambu flying out at dawn to bring back red paddy and returning at evening.
links.teaches: Both describe food coming into Parambu without its people farming, which suggests the self-feeding hill was a known part of Pari's legend that an akam poet could use as a ready simile for something sure to return.

links.note: 110 tells the three kings that Parambu is hard to take though they join forces; Akananuru 78 recalls Pari, with Kapilar beside him, driving off the tusked kings after years of fighting.
links.teaches: The akam poem treats as settled history what 110 states as a boast during the siege, so the pair shows the defence of Parambu passing from Kapilar's own war-speech into the shared stock of akam similes.

links.note: 111 says the hill cannot be won by kings with the spear and only a singer can have it; 112 says kings with victorious drums have taken our hill.
links.teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the boast that the hill could not be taken and the daughters' report that it was taken show how the editors let the poems record the siege's outcome against Kapilar's claim.

links.note: Naladiyar 3 says even kings who led armies under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and their enemies take their wives; 112 has a giver's daughters say the kings took their hill and they have no father.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar explains a ruler's fall by his own spent deeds, but 112 gives no cause and its subject is a famous giver, so the lament qualifies the moral account: here loss falls on the blameless and the poem does not explain it.

links.note: 113 ends with Kapilar leaving Parambu to find husbands for Pari's daughters; in 200 he offers them in marriage to Vichikko.
links.teaches: The two poems give the beginning and a later stage of one errand: the lament's last line becomes a formal offer in 200, which shows the duty of the dead patron's poet carried out as a sequence of poems.

links.note: 109 predicts that the besieging kings will not take Parambu by force; 116 recalls that the daughters once counted from the hill the horses of kings who came to fight without knowing Pari's strength, and now count salt carts.
links.teaches: Read after 109, 116 shows what the confident siege-speech left out: the kings did come, and the poet who promised the fort was safe now measures its fall by what the daughters count.

links.note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a ruler who wields the sceptre rightly; 117 says Pari's land never lacked rain, even under the omens of drought, because of the straightness of his sceptre.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule is given to crowned kings, and 117 grants it to a hill chief and sets it above the stars' omens, so the poem shows the doctrine of the just sceptre extended to any lord who rules well.

links.note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of a kindly man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 119 likens Pari to a lone tree on a long road without shade.
links.teaches: The Kural puts its tree where everyone can reach it, while 119 puts it where nothing else gives shelter, so the poem adds that a giver's worth is measured by how few others give.

links.note: Both lists of the land's harvest break off with the same question, நந்துங் கொல்லோ (will it last?), before naming the land as the dead patron's.
links.teaches: The shared refrain shows the poems were made as a set in which each catalogue of plenty is undercut by the same doubt, so the anthology's sequence on Pari works like a song with a refrain.

new_concepts.gloss: the guide poem, one performer directing another to a patron
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai விறலியாற்றுப்படை of 103 and 105, and 109 lines 15 to 17, which use the form against the besieging kings

new_concepts.gloss: the state of helpless grief after a patron's or lord's death, and the lament that voices it

source_issues: 101, 113 and 117: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line. In each our line 1 is needed for the sense (101: the first of the counted visits; 113: the toddy and the rams that the next line continues; 117: the first of the three omens), so the site has dropped or merged a line; all lines are marked.

116: the review's line table says we lack the site's line 10, after our line 9; the poem's middle (lines 9 to 14) does not read smoothly, consistent with a lost line. Marked as it stands and flagged uncertain.
116 line 9 (நோகோ யானே; தேய்கமா காலை!) is flagged as repeated in 234 line 1; it reads as a formula of grief shared by two laments, not a copying error.
110 line 2: கொள்ற்கு looks like a misprint for கொளற்கு (to take).

109: the colophon thurai மகண் மறுத்தல் is the sandhi spelling of மகள் மறுத்தல், as in 110 and 111; normalised in puram_thurai name. None of 109 to 111 mentions a daughter; the thurai comes from the tradition of the siege.
112: the colophon thurai is written கையறு நிலை, while 113 to 120 have கையறுநிலை; the same thurai.
117 line 8: முள் லெயிறு is முள்ளெயிறு (sharp tooth) split at an odd point.
102: the poem names no one; the patron Pokuttezhini is known only from the colophon.
113 to 120: the colophon patron is None, though every poem is about Pari; the poems name him (116, 118) or call him the girls' father (117, 120).
